a: Once we had been pulled away from them
p: The verb is a strong one. Leaving the Ephesian elders hurt.
b: The Greek apospasthentas means "pulled away, torn away," the word for drawing a sword from its sheath (Matthew 26:51) or for Jesus withdrawing from his disciples in Gethsemane (Luke 22:41). Coming straight after the tearful goodbye at Miletus, where the elders wept and kissed Paul because they would never see him again (20:37–38), it tells the reader that the ship did not simply leave. The travelers had to wrench themselves free. The "we" of the narrator, which began again at 20:5, runs through this whole journey to Jerusalem and stops at 21:18.

a: Cos
p: Cos, Rhodes and Patara were normal stops for ships working down the coast of Asia Minor.
b: Coasting ships in the eastern Mediterranean usually sailed by day and anchored at night. Cos and Rhodes are islands off the southwest corner of today's Turkey, about a day apart. Patara, on the coast of Lycia, was a large harbor with a famous oracle of Apollo; a lighthouse built there under Nero has been excavated. At Patara the travelers changed ships. Instead of creeping along the shore, they took a bigger ship going straight across the open sea to Phoenicia, a run of about 400 miles, which with the steady northwest winds of early summer could take as little as four or five days. Paul was hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (20:16).

a: Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to set foot in Jerusalem
p: The disciples speak "through the Spirit," yet Paul goes anyway. Readers have long asked how both can be right.
b:
Paul had already said he was going to Jerusalem "bound in the Spirit," and that in every city the Holy Spirit warned him that chains were waiting (20:22–23). Now the disciples at Tyre tell him "through the Spirit" not to go. Three main readings:
  • Revelation and inference. The most common view (Chrysostom, Bruce, Keener): the Spirit showed them the suffering ahead, and out of love they drew the conclusion that he should not go. Agabus' prophecy (21:11) has the same pattern: the Spirit foretells, the friends plead.
  • A real command, disobeyed. A minority hold that Paul went against the Spirit's warning and that his arrest was the result.
  • A test. Some read the warnings as God giving Paul a free choice, which he made with open eyes (21:13).
Luke's own frame favors the first: Paul's going is the Lord's will (21:14; 23:11).

a: We went down on our knees on the shore
p: Jews usually prayed standing. Luke notes kneeling at moments of crisis.
b: Standing was the ordinary posture of prayer in Jewish and early Christian practice (Matthew 6:5; Mark 11:25). Luke mentions kneeling at turning points: Jesus in the garden (Luke 22:41), Stephen as he died (7:60), Peter at Tabitha's bed (9:40), Paul with the Ephesian elders (20:36), and now a whole church, wives and children too, on the beach at Tyre. The scene is the second of three farewells on the way to Jerusalem, each sadder than the last.

a: Ptolemais
p: The old Canaanite port of Acco, renamed by the Ptolemies, today's Akko north of Haifa.
b: Acco was an ancient harbor on the bay north of Mount Carmel (Judges 1:31). After Alexander the Great it was renamed Ptolemais by the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt, and the emperor Claudius made it a colony for retired Roman soldiers. That there were already "brothers" there fits Luke's earlier note that believers scattered after Stephen's death went as far as Phoenicia (11:19). From here the party went on by land or by a short coastal run to Caesarea, about 35 miles south.

a: Philip the evangelist
p: This is the Philip of chapters 6 and 8, one of the Seven, who settled in Caesarea.
b: Luke last left Philip arriving at Caesarea after baptizing the Ethiopian official (8:40). That was perhaps twenty years earlier. He had been chosen as one of the Seven to serve the Greek-speaking widows (6:5) and had become the first to take the good news to Samaria (8:5–13). "Evangelist" (euangelistēs, "one who tells the good news") appears only three times in the New Testament: here, in Ephesians 4:11 among the gifts Christ gave the church, and in 2 Timothy 4:5. Luke takes care to say he is Philip "of the Seven," since there was also Philip the apostle (1:13). Later writers sometimes confused the two.

a: four daughters, virgins who prophesied
p: Luke names four women prophets and then gives none of them a word to say. Why mention them?
b: The daughters fulfill Joel's promise quoted at Pentecost, that "your daughters will prophesy" (2:17). "Virgins" (parthenoi) means they were unmarried, probably young; the word does not by itself mean a lifelong vow. Later Christians remembered them well. Papias of Hierapolis heard stories from them, and Polycrates of Ephesus (about AD 190) said two were buried at Hierapolis and another at Ephesus (Eusebius, Church History 3.31; 3.39). The Montanist prophets of the second century claimed them as forerunners. Readers differ on why Luke reports no oracle from them. Some think he simply moves to Agabus, whose sign is dramatic; some see a sign of Luke's restraint toward women's speech; others note that Luke treats their prophesying as a settled fact that needed no defense. On what the churches draw from this verse, see the Where Christians differ card.

a: a prophet by the name of Agabus
p: The same prophet foretold the famine in 11:28. His word had come true before.
b: Luke introduces Agabus as if for the first time, which some take as a sign that Luke used different sources for chapter 11 and this one. But the reader already knows him: he came down from Jerusalem to Antioch and foretold, by the Spirit, a severe famine, which happened under Claudius (11:27–28). A prophet with a record of accurate predictions now speaks about Paul. That makes his warning hard to wave away, and Paul does not deny it. He only refuses to let it stop him.

a: bound his own feet and hands with it
p: Agabus acts out his message, like Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and introduces it with a messenger formula.
b: Israel's prophets often acted their words: Isaiah walked stripped like a captive (Isaiah 20:2–4), Jeremiah buried a linen belt and dug it up ruined (Jeremiah 13:1–11), Ezekiel lay bound with ropes (Ezekiel 4:4–8). Agabus' bound hands and feet are the same kind of sign. His opening, "The Holy Spirit says this," copies the prophets' "The LORD says this" and puts the Spirit in the place of the LORD. The same Greek formula opens each of the seven letters in Revelation (Revelation 2:1).

a: the Jews in Jerusalem will bind him just like this
t: Did Agabus get the details right?
p: In the event, Roman soldiers put Paul in chains (21:33), while the Jewish crowd tried to kill him.
b: Read with wooden literalness, the prophecy misses: the Jews in the temple seized and beat Paul, but the commander had him bound with two chains and took him from them (21:30–33). Readers answer this in several ways. Many say the prophecy is true in substance: Paul's own later summary is that he was handed over from Jerusalem as a prisoner into Roman hands (28:17), so the Jews' action led to Roman chains. Some see a sign that New Testament prophecy, unlike the words of the Old Testament prophets, could be inspired yet imprecise in detail (Wayne Grudem's view; others reject it). Many literary readers notice that the words echo Jesus' prediction that the Son of Man would be handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32), and think Luke wanted the echo more than a precise forecast.

a: For the name of the Lord Jesus I am prepared to be bound in Jerusalem
p: Luke tells Paul's last journey to Jerusalem in a way that recalls Jesus' own.
b: Jesus set out for Jerusalem knowing what waited there (Luke 9:51); so does Paul. Jesus foretold that he would be handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32); so does Agabus. Jesus' friends tried to turn him from suffering (Matthew 16:22); Paul's friends weep and beg. Peter once told Jesus he was ready to go with him to prison and to death (Luke 22:33), and failed; Paul says the same and keeps his word. The parallels run on: a temple scene, a crowd crying "Away with him!" (21:36), hearings before the Sanhedrin, a Roman governor and a Herod, and declarations of innocence. Luke never says Paul's suffering saves anyone. He shows the disciple walking the road his Lord walked.

a: May the Lord's will be done
p: The friends end with words that recall Jesus' prayer: "May your will be done" (Matthew 6:10).
b: The Greek tou kyriou to thelēma ginesthō is close to the Lord's Prayer, "May your will be done" (Matthew 6:10), and to Jesus' prayer the night before he died, that his Father's will be done and not his own (Luke 22:42). Here "the Lord" is most likely Jesus, named in the verse before. The friends stop arguing, not because they have been proved wrong, but because they hand the matter over to him.

a: the man who would be our host
p: The Greek can mean they brought Paul to Mnason's house, or that they brought Mnason along with them.
b: The clause agontes par' hō xenisthōmen Mnasōni literally reads "bringing [someone] with whom we might lodge, Mnason." Most translations take it to mean that the Caesarean disciples led the party to Mnason's home. Others read it as "bringing Mnason with them," so that he traveled from Caesarea as their host-to-be. Either way, Mnason was a Cypriot believer "from the early days," perhaps converted at Pentecost or soon after, and willing to house a group that included Gentiles (20:4). Codex Bezae (05) has a longer reading in which the party stops on the way at a village where the host lives (see the variants). That would make the 65-mile trip a two-day journey, which fits the distance.
orig: ἄγοντες παρ' ᾧ ξενισθῶμεν Μνάσωνι (agontes par' hō xenisthōmen Mnasōni)

a: Paul went with us to visit James
p: James leads the Jerusalem church. He was known for keeping the law, and was killed in AD 62.
b: This is James the brother of Jesus (Galatians 1:19), not the apostle James son of Zebedee, whom Herod Agrippa I had killed (12:2). He became the leading figure in the Jerusalem church (12:17; 15:13–21; Galatians 2:9, 12). Later tradition called him "James the Just" for his strict devotion to the law and the temple. Josephus says the high priest Ananus had him stoned in AD 62, in the gap between two Roman governors, and that law-observant Jews in Jerusalem were angry at it (Antiquities 20.200–203). Luke never calls James an apostle, never says what he thought of Paul's collection money (see the chapter page), and never mentions him again after this scene.

a: went with us
p: Here the narrator's "we" stops until 27:1. Readers disagree about what the "we" means.
b: The second "we" passage (20:5–21:18) ends as Paul goes in to James. It returns only when Paul sails for Rome (27:1). On what the "we" means, see the book's opening pages. The usual readings: an eyewitness author, traditionally Luke, who was with Paul on this journey (Irenaeus; Hemer; Keener); a travel diary or source that the author used; or a literary device that gives the account the feel of being there (Pervo and others). If the author was present, he was in Judea during Paul's two years in custody at Caesarea (24:27), which would explain the detail in chapters 21–26.

a: how many tens of thousands among the Jews have come to believe
p: The Greek is myriades, "myriads." Readers argue whether it means real numbers or a loose "thousands."
b: A myrias is ten thousand, and the plural is often used loosely for a huge number, as in Luke 12:1, where "the myriads of the crowd" gather. Some take James' words literally, which would make the believing Jews of Judea a very large movement by the late 50s. Others think they mean "thousands" (as many English Bibles have it), or that they include pilgrims in the city for Pentecost. Either way the elders' point is not the size but the character of the movement: "all of them zealous for the law." The church of Jerusalem was Jewish, and proudly so.

a: zealous for the law
t: Jewish believers who kept the law
p: The Jerusalem church kept the law of Moses, and Luke presents this as a good thing.
b: The elders praise God for Paul's report and in the same breath describe their own people as "zealous for the law." Luke does not treat this as a fault. Jewish believers in Jesus kept the Sabbath, circumcised their sons and worshiped in the temple (2:46; 3:1; 10:14). The word "zealous" (zēlōtai) could have sharper overtones. In the decades before the revolt against Rome, "zeal for the law" in the tradition of Phinehas could justify violence (Numbers 25:11; 1 Maccabees 2:26), and during the war of 66–70 one party called themselves the Zealots (Josephus, Jewish War 4). Martin Hengel traced this tradition of zeal. Jacob Jervell argued that for Luke the church is restored Israel, with law-keeping Jews at its center and Gentiles added. Others think Luke shows a stage the church was leaving behind. The verse is important in Jewish-Christian dialogue, because it shows that following Jesus and keeping the law were not felt to be opposites by the first believers.

a: to desert Moses
t: Was the rumor about Paul true?
p: Paul was said to teach Jews to give up circumcision and the law. His letters can be read on both sides.
b:
The Greek is "you teach apostasy from Moses." Luke presents the charge as false: the elders say the reports "amount to nothing" (21:24), and Paul later says he has done nothing against the people or the customs (28:17). His letters complicate the picture. He told Gentiles they must not be circumcised (Galatians 5:2), but told Jews not to undo theirs (1 Corinthians 7:18), and said that to Jews he became like a Jew, to win them (1 Corinthians 9:20). He called the law holy (Romans 7:12) but said no one is put right with God by its works (Galatians 2:16). Three readings:
  • The rumor was false. Paul never told Jews to stop keeping the law; he only refused to impose it on Gentiles. This is the "Paul within Judaism" view (Nanos, Fredriksen) and also Luke's.
  • Half true. Paul taught that the law no longer defined God's people, and Jews who took his teaching seriously would loosen their observance (many Protestant readers, Barrett).
  • Luke smooths Paul. Critical scholars since Vielhauer have argued that Acts makes Paul more law-observant than his letters do.
orig: ἀποστασίαν διδάσκεις ἀπὸ Μωϋσέως (apostasian didaskeis apo Mōuseōs)

a: they have been told things about you
p: The verb is katēcheō, the word behind "catechism." Luke used it of Theophilus' own instruction.
b: Katēchēthēsan means "they have been informed" but often "they have been taught," by repeated telling. It is the same verb Luke used in his preface: Theophilus had been "instructed" in the faith (Luke 1:4), and Apollos had been instructed in the way of the Lord in the same sense (18:25). Here the believers in Judea had been systematically "taught" a wrong picture of Paul. The choice of word suggests a campaign, not a stray rumor. The Christian word "catechism" comes from this verb.

a: Four men among us have taken a vow on themselves
p: The four men were almost certainly under a Nazirite vow, which ended with offerings and shaving the head.
b: A Nazirite vowed for a set time to drink no wine, cut no hair and avoid any dead body (Numbers 6:1–8). At the end he offered a lamb, a ewe lamb and a ram with grain and drink offerings, and "the Nazirite will shave off the hair he dedicated" (Numbers 6:18) and burn it under the peace offering. Three animals with their grain and drink offerings, for each of four men, cost a good deal, and paying a poor Nazirite's costs was a known act of piety: Josephus says King Agrippa I, on arriving in Jerusalem, paid for very many Nazirites to have their heads shaved (Antiquities 19.294). The elders ask Paul to do the same for four men, publicly, in the temple. Compare the vow at Cenchreae in 18:18.

a: go through the purification together with them
p: Paul was not a Nazirite. He seems to have gone through a seven-day cleansing of his own.
b: The verb hagnisthēti means "be purified." A Nazirite vow could not be begun and ended in a week; at least thirty days was normal in later Jewish practice (Mishnah Nazir 1:3). So Paul probably did not join the vow. Two other explanations are given. Many think Paul, coming back from long years in Gentile lands, underwent the seven-day purification from corpse impurity, with sprinkling on the third and seventh days (Numbers 19:12), so that he could enter the inner courts with the four men. Others think the four men had become unclean during their vow and had to be purified and restart, and Paul joined their cleansing as their sponsor. Either way, the "seven days" of 21:27 fit.

a: walk in line with the law
p: The verb stoicheō, "walk in line," is a word Paul himself uses in his letters.
b: Stoicheō pictures soldiers in a rank or plants in a row: "stay in line, walk in step." Outside Acts it appears only in Paul's letters, where he uses it for walking in step with the Spirit (Galatians 5:25), following a rule (Galatians 6:16; Philippians 3:16), and walking in the footsteps of Abraham's faith (Romans 4:12). The elders want people to see Paul walking in step with Moses. Whether Paul could honestly do this has divided Christian readers since Augustine and Jerome argued about it (see the chapter page).

a: Now concerning the believers from the Gentiles
t: Why repeat the decree to Paul?
p: James and the elders recall the Jerusalem decree of 15:20, 29 as if Paul had not heard it. Some think he had not.
b: Paul was present when the decree was agreed and carried it to the churches (15:22–30; 16:4). So why do James and the elders (the Greek verb is plural, "we") tell him again? Most readers take it as reassurance: the elders are not asking anything new of Gentile believers; the request is only for Jewish believers like Paul himself. Some critical scholars read it differently. Paul's letters never mention the decree, and in 1 Corinthians 8–10 he handles food offered to idols without appealing to it. In Galatians 2:6 he says the Jerusalem leaders added nothing to his message. So some argue that Paul did not know of the decree, which was made later or without him, and that Luke's source here is closer to the facts than chapter 15. On the decree's four items and its Western form, see 15:20 and 15:29.

a: the offering would be brought for each one of them
t: A follower of Jesus offering sacrifice
p: Paul pays for temple sacrifices some twenty-five years after the cross. Luke tells it without embarrassment.
b: The offerings for a Nazirite included a sin offering (Numbers 6:14). That Paul, the apostle of the cross, would sponsor sacrifices in the temple has troubled some Christian readers, since Hebrews teaches that Christ's sacrifice made the old offerings obsolete (Hebrews 10:11–18). Luke shows no unease: the first believers prayed in the temple daily (2:46; 3:1), and Paul later tells Felix that he came to Jerusalem to bring gifts for the poor of his nation and to present offerings (24:17). Many scholars, Jewish and Christian, see this as evidence that the earliest Jewish believers saw no conflict between faith in Jesus and temple worship. Others say the sacrifices were for vows and thanks, not for sin, though Numbers 6:14 includes a sin offering, so the point is debated.

a: the Jews from Asia
p: Jews from the province of Asia, in Jerusalem for Pentecost, knew Paul from Ephesus.
b: "Asia" is the Roman province in the west of today's Turkey, with Ephesus its chief city. Paul had worked there for more than two years (19:10), had been thrown out of its synagogue (19:8–9) and had reminded the Ephesian elders of the trials that plots by Jews there had brought him (20:19). Pilgrims from Asia came up for Pentecost (2:9), and some of these recognized him, and his companion Trophimus, an Ephesian (21:29). The same group of Jews from Asia, with others from Cilicia, had once disputed with Stephen (6:9). Luke is careful here: the trouble begins with a particular group, not with the people of Jerusalem or the elders of the church.

a: made this holy place common
t: The warning stone in the temple
p: Stone notices in Greek and Latin warned Gentiles not to pass into the inner courts on pain of death. Two have been found.
b: The temple's outer court was open to everyone. A low stone barrier (the soreg) marked off the inner courts, and notices set along it threatened death to any foreigner who went in (Josephus, Jewish War 5.193–194; Antiquities 15.417; compare Philo, Embassy 212). In 1871 Charles Clermont-Ganneau found one of them, complete, in Jerusalem; it is now in Istanbul. A broken second copy was found in 1935 and is in the Israel Museum. The complete one says, in Greek, that no foreigner may enter within the barrier and enclosure around the sanctuary, and whoever is caught will be to blame for his own death that follows. Josephus has Titus say that Rome let the Jews enforce this even on Roman citizens (Jewish War 6.126). The Greek verb here, kekoinōken, "has made common," is the same word for "common" that Peter refused in his vision (10:14–15). Paul's opponents accused him of bringing Trophimus past this line.

a: against the people, against the law and against this place
p: The accusation repeats almost word for word the charge that led to Stephen's death.
b: False witnesses said that Stephen never stopped speaking against the holy place and the law (6:13). Behind both stands the charge at Jesus' trial that he would destroy the temple (Mark 14:58; Matthew 26:61). Luke lets the reader hear the old accusation in a new mouth. Paul, who once guarded the cloaks of Stephen's killers (22:20), now hears the same words aimed at himself, from the same kind of opponents, Diaspora Jews (6:9).

a: Trophimus, a man from Ephesus
p: A Gentile believer from Ephesus who traveled with Paul to deliver the collection.
b: Trophimus is listed among the delegates from the churches who went with Paul (20:4), probably carrying Asia's share of the collection for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). He appears again, left sick at Miletus, in 2 Timothy 4:20. The accusers had seen him with Paul in the city and "took it for granted," the Greek enomizon, "they supposed," that Paul had brought him into the inner courts. Luke makes clear that the charge rests on an assumption.

a: the doors were shut
p: The Levite gatekeepers shut the gates to the inner courts. Many readers see a symbol: the temple closes on Paul.
b: On the surface the act is practical. The Levites who guarded the temple shut the gates between the inner courts and the outer court, so that a killing, if it came, would not defile the sanctuary. But Luke's story of the temple is a long one. His Gospel opens and closes in the temple (Luke 1:8–9; 24:53), and the first believers met there daily (Acts 2:46). After this verse no believer enters the temple again in Acts. Many interpreters read the shut doors as a quiet sign that the temple has closed itself to the message. Others caution that Luke is reporting an incident, and that he still has Paul honor the temple (24:11–12, 18).

a: the commander of the cohort
p: A Roman tribune commanded a cohort, a unit of up to a thousand men, in the Antonia fortress beside the temple.
b: The Greek chiliarchos means "commander of a thousand," the Latin tribunus. A speira (cohort) was nominally a thousand men, often fewer, and the one in Jerusalem was an auxiliary unit, mostly recruited from non-Jews in the region. It was based in the Antonia, a fortress Herod built at the northwest corner of the temple and named for Mark Antony. During festivals soldiers stood on the roofs of the porticoes to watch the crowds (Josephus, Jewish War 2.224; 5.244). That is why the commander could "charge down" so fast. We learn his name, Claudius Lysias, only from his letter (23:26).

a: the stairs
p: Josephus describes stairs leading from the temple porticoes up into the Antonia. Paul spoke from them.
b: Josephus says that where the Antonia met the porticoes of the temple it had stairs going down to both, by which the guards came down (Jewish War 5.243). From these steps, above the heads of the crowd and under the soldiers' protection, Paul gives his speech. The scene is vivid: a battered prisoner in chains, carried by soldiers because the crowd would tear him apart, turns at the top of the stairs and asks to speak.

a: Away with him!
p: The crowd shouts nearly the same Greek words the crowd shouted against Jesus.
b: The cry Aire auton, "Take him away!", is nearly what the crowd shouted before Pilate. The closest match is in Luke's Gospel, where the crowd cries aire touton, "take this man away" (Luke 23:18). John has another form of the same verb (aron, aron): "Away with him! Away! Crucify him!" (John 19:15). Luke lets the echo stand without comment, one more way Paul's story follows his Lord's (see 21:13). The crowd repeats the cry, in fuller form, at 22:22.

a: You know Greek?
p: The commander is surprised that his prisoner speaks educated Greek. Paul will address the crowd in Hebrew.
b: Jerusalem was a city of several languages. Aramaic was the everyday speech of Judea, Hebrew the language of Scripture and prayer, Greek the language of trade, government and the many Jews from abroad, and Latin the language of the Roman army's officers. A Roman tribune would speak Greek, the common language of the eastern empire. He assumed that a rioter in the temple would not, and it may have been Paul's educated Greek, as much as what he said, that made him think again.

a: that Egyptian
p: Josephus tells of an Egyptian false prophet whom Felix routed. The commander thought Paul was that man come back.
b: Josephus tells the story twice. An Egyptian who claimed to be a prophet gathered followers in the wilderness and led them to the Mount of Olives, promising that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command. The governor Felix attacked with troops, killed or captured many, and the Egyptian escaped (Jewish War 2.261–263; Antiquities 20.169–172). This happened around AD 54–56, a few years before Paul's arrest. Josephus gives 30,000 followers in one account and 400 killed and 200 captured in the other; the commander's "four thousand" is smaller and may be closer to the truth, since Josephus often inflates numbers. Whether Luke used Josephus or both drew on common knowledge is debated; the differences suggest independent reports.

a: the four thousand men of the Sicarii
p: Sicarii is Latin for "dagger men," assassins who stabbed their targets in the festival crowds.
b: The Greek borrows the Latin sicarii, from sica, a short curved dagger. Josephus says that under Felix a new kind of bandit appeared in Jerusalem who killed people in broad daylight, especially at festivals, hiding small daggers under their clothes and melting into the crowd. Their first victim was the former high priest Jonathan (Jewish War 2.254–257). Josephus does not link them to the Egyptian, so the commander's phrase may lump together the troublemakers of the day. English Bibles vary: "Assassins," "terrorists," "murderers" (KJV). This translation keeps their name so readers can find them in history books.

a: a citizen of a city that is far from unknown
p: Tarsus was a proud, wealthy city with famous schools. Paul answers the commander with a polished turn of phrase.
b: Tarsus, capital of Cilicia in southern Turkey, stood on the Cydnus River on a major trade route. The geographer Strabo praised its schools of philosophy and rhetoric, which he said outdid those of Athens and Alexandria in eagerness for learning (Geography 14.5.13). "No obscure city" is a stylish understatement found in Greek writers; commentators compare a line in Euripides' Ion. Being a "citizen" of Tarsus meant membership in the city's body of citizens, distinct from the Roman citizenship Paul will reveal in 22:25–28. Some scholars doubt a Jew could easily be both, but Jewish communities in Greek cities did contain citizens, and Luke's account is widely accepted.

a: in Hebrew
p: The Greek says "in the Hebrew dialect." Most scholars think Aramaic is meant; some argue for Hebrew.
b: Tē Hebraidi dialektō is literally "in the Hebrew language." Many English Bibles print "Aramaic," because Aramaic was the everyday speech of Judea, and Greek writers often called it "Hebrew" (John 19:13, 17 use "Hebrew" for Aramaic place names such as Gabbatha and Golgotha). A growing number of scholars, pointing to Hebrew texts among the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Bar Kokhba letters, think Hebrew was still spoken and may be meant here. This translation keeps "Hebrew," as the Greek says. The effect is the same either way: Paul speaks to them in their own tongue, and the crowd falls silent (22:2).

a: my defense
t: The first of Paul's defense speeches
p: The Greek apologia is a courtroom word. From here to chapter 26, Paul is always on trial.
b: Apologia means a speech in one's own defense, the word behind "apologetics." It marks the start of a new section of Acts. Paul will make five defenses: to the crowd (22:1–21), to the Sanhedrin (23:1–6), to Felix (24:10–21), to Festus (25:8–11) and to Agrippa (26:1–29). Jesus had told his followers they would be brought before synagogues, rulers and authorities, and not to worry about how they would make their defense (Luke 12:11–12; Luke 21:12–15, the same word). "Brothers and fathers" is how Stephen began his speech before the council (7:2).

a: born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but I grew up here in this city
p: Three verbs, born, brought up, educated, may mean Paul came to Jerusalem as a small child.
b: W. C. van Unnik pointed out that "born... brought up... trained" (gegennēmenos... anatethrammenos... pepaideumenos) was a standard Greek sequence for the stages of a life: birth, upbringing in the home, then schooling. If Luke uses it that way, Paul was raised in Jerusalem from early childhood, not just sent there as a student, and Aramaic and the Jewish ways of the capital were his from the start. Others think the phrase is looser and that Paul's fluent Greek and knowledge of the Greek Bible suggest a longer youth in Tarsus. Paul's letters do not settle it; he speaks of advancing in Judaism beyond his peers (Galatians 1:14) but never names Gamaliel.

a: I sat at the feet of Gamaliel
p: Gamaliel the Elder was the most honored teacher of his day. "At the feet" is how students sat.
b: Gamaliel, already met in 5:34–39, was a leading Pharisee, remembered in Jewish tradition as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. The Mishnah says that when he died "the glory of the Torah ceased, and purity and separateness died" (Mishnah Sotah 9:15). Students sat on the ground before a seated teacher; a saying in Mishnah Avot 1:4 urges, "sit in the dust of their feet." Some scholars doubt that Paul studied with him, since his letters never say so, and since Gamaliel's caution in 5:34–39 contrasts with Paul's violence. Others reply that a teacher's students need not share his temper, and that naming Gamaliel to this crowd would have been easy to disprove if false.

a: I was zealous for God, the same as every one of you is today
p: Paul does not attack the crowd's zeal. He says he once had the same zeal, and it made him a persecutor.
b: Paul writes that his zeal once made him a persecutor of the church (Philippians 3:6), and that he was more zealous than others his age for the traditions of his ancestors (Galatians 1:14). The model of zeal in Jewish memory was Phinehas, who killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman to stop a plague (Numbers 25:7–13), and Elijah (1 Kings 19:10). By saying "the same as every one of you is today," Paul treats the riot that nearly killed him as zeal for God, misdirected as his own once was. It is generous, and it is also his whole argument: what changed him was not lack of zeal but meeting Jesus.

a: this Way
p: The first believers called their movement "the Way."
b: Acts uses "the Way" as a name for the movement (9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14, 22). It may come from Isaiah's "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (Isaiah 40:3), a verse the community at Qumran also used to describe itself as those who walk in "the way." Paul uses the name before a Jewish crowd as if it were one more group within Israel, like the Pharisees or the Essenes. On the name and "the sect of the Nazarenes," see 24:5, 14.

a: The high priest will back me up on this
p: The high priest who sent Saul to Damascus was not the one in office now. Readers explain the present tense in different ways.
b: Saul's letters came from the high priest of the mid-30s, probably Caiaphas (until about AD 36) or his successor Jonathan, son of Annas (9:1). The high priest in 57 or so was Ananias son of Nedebaeus (23:2). Most commentators take Paul to mean the high-priestly office and its records: the council's archives, and older members still sitting in the Sanhedrin, could confirm what he did. Some think Luke has simply written loosely. Either way Paul's claim is bold: his own enemies are his witnesses.

a: letters from them addressed to the brothers in Damascus
p: "The brothers" here are fellow Jews in Damascus. The letters asked the synagogues there to help Saul.
b: In his speech to Jews, Paul calls the Jews of Damascus "the brothers." Whether the high priest had legal power to have people arrested in another province is doubted. Many historians think the letters were not warrants Rome would enforce but requests that the synagogues cooperate, which they could do within their own discipline, as Paul himself later suffered synagogue floggings (2 Corinthians 11:24). Damascus then had a large Jewish community; Josephus says thousands of its Jews were killed there in AD 66 (Jewish War 2.559–561).

a: around midday
p: Acts tells Paul's call three times (9, 22, 26). Each adds or changes details.
b: Only this telling and 26:13 give the time, "around midday," when the sun was brightest, so the light was brighter still. The three accounts differ in other ways: in chapter 9 the men with Saul hear the voice but see no one (9:7); here they see the light but do not hear the voice (22:9); in chapter 26 all fall to the ground (26:14), and Jesus gives Paul his commission directly, with no Ananias. Readers explain the differences as natural variation in retelling (ancient historians shaped each telling for its hearers), as signs of different sources, or as Luke's deliberate art, each version fitted to its audience. See the chapter page.

a: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?
p: A doubled name is how God calls people in the Hebrew Bible. Jesus calls Saul by his Hebrew name.
b: "Abraham! Abraham!" (Genesis 22:11), "Jacob, Jacob" (Genesis 46:2), "Moses! Moses!" (Exodus 3:4), "Samuel! Samuel!" (1 Samuel 3:10): the doubled name marks a call from God. The Greek here spells the name Saoul, the Hebrew form, not the Greek Saulos, which fits the voice speaking "in Hebrew" (26:14). The words are the same in all three accounts (9:4; 26:14). Jesus asks why Saul persecutes "me," not "my followers": to harm the church is to harm him. The church fathers saw here the root of Paul's teaching that believers are the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:27).

a: I am Jesus the Nazarene
p: Only this telling adds "the Nazarene." It is the name the crowd would know.
b: In 9:5 and 26:15 the voice says simply "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting." Here, speaking to a Jerusalem crowd, Paul gives the fuller name Iēsous ho Nazōraios, the title on the cross (John 19:19) and the name used of Jesus by his enemies and his followers alike (2:22; 3:6; 4:10). Christians were later called "the sect of the Nazarenes" (24:5).

a: the voice of the one who spoke to me they did not hear
t: Did the men hear the voice or not?
p: 9:7 says they heard the voice; here they did not. Many translations say "did not understand." Is that right?
b: In 9:7 the companions are "hearing the voice" (akouontes tēs phōnēs, genitive case); here they "did not hear the voice" (tēn phōnēn ouk ēkousan, accusative). An old explanation says the genitive means hearing a sound and the accusative means hearing with understanding, so the men heard a noise but not words. That is why some English Bibles have "did not understand" here. Many Greek scholars doubt the rule holds; Luke himself breaks it elsewhere. But the verb akouō can mean "understand" (1 Corinthians 14:2), and the context, "the voice of the one who spoke to me," fits that sense. Other readers think Luke simply did not mind a loose detail between tellings, since his point in both is the same: the companions were witnesses that something happened, but the message was for Paul alone.
orig: τὴν δὲ φωνὴν οὐκ ἤκουσαν (tēn de phōnēn ouk ēkousan)

a: The glory of that light
p: Paul says "glory" (doxa), not just brightness. The word ties his call to God's glory in the Scriptures.
b: The Greek doxa can mean brightness, but in the Bible it is the word for God's visible glory: the glory that filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and shone from Moses' face (Exodus 34:29–35). Paul's letters return to this moment in those terms: the God who made light shine in darkness has shone in believers' hearts, giving the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6); and Paul claims to have seen Jesus the Lord (1 Corinthians 9:1). Paul, the zealous man, was blinded by the glory he had been defending.

a: He was devout, as the law measures it
t: A different Ananias for a different audience
p: In chapter 9 Ananias is "a disciple." Here he is a law-keeping Jew respected by all the Jews of Damascus.
b: In 9:10 Ananias is a disciple who receives a vision from the Lord. To this crowd Paul introduces him only as "devout, as the law measures it," with a good name among "every Jew living in Damascus," and does not call him a Christian at all. This is one of the clearest signs that the speeches are shaped for their hearers. Ancient historians and orators were expected to do this, and Paul says in his letters that he did it himself (1 Corinthians 9:20). Critical readers take it as Luke's composition; others as Paul's own good sense before a mob that had just accused him of attacking the law. Both agree on the effect: the man who healed Paul was the kind of Jew the crowd respected.

a: see again
p: The verb anablepō means both "look up" and "regain sight." Paul does both at once.
b: Anablepson can mean "see again" (it is used for the healing of the blind, Luke 18:41–43) or simply "look up" (Luke 19:5). Here both senses work together. Ananias tells Saul to see again, and the same verb in the next sentence, aneblepsa, says both that Saul's sight came back and that his first act with restored eyes was to look up at Ananias; the Plain gives both. The healing matches 9:17–18, where Saul's sight comes back. Luke's Gospel opened Jesus' ministry with a promise of sight for the blind (Luke 4:18, quoting the Greek of Isaiah 61:1), and Paul's commission will be to open the eyes of the nations (26:18).

a: to see the Righteous One
p: A title for Jesus used by Peter and Stephen. It echoes the righteous servant of Isaiah 53.
b: Peter accused the people of denying "the Holy and Righteous One" (3:14), and Stephen said the prophets foretold the coming of the Righteous One (7:52). The title recalls the suffering servant: "the righteous one, my servant, will make the many righteous" (Isaiah 53:11), and the righteous man of Wisdom of Solomon 2:12–20 (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians), mocked and killed by the wicked. Other Jewish writings use the title too: the Parables of Enoch, which only the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts as Scripture, call the coming judge "the Righteous One" (1 Enoch 38:2). Ananias, a devout Jew, uses a Jewish title for Jesus. The verb "chose" is procheirizomai, "choose, select, appoint," used again at 26:16 ("to choose you") and of Jesus at 3:20. Despite its prefix pro-, it does not here mean "choose in advance."
r: 3:14, 20; 7:52; 26:16; Isaiah 53:11; Wisdom of Solomon 2:12–20; 1 Enoch 38:2; 1 John 2:1

a: have your sins washed away
p: Ananias ties baptism, washing away sins and calling on Jesus' name in one sentence. Churches read the link differently.
b: Both verbs are in the Greek middle voice: baptisai, "get yourself baptized," and apolousai, "get your sins washed away." The participle "calling on his name" echoes Joel's promise that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Joel 2:32), taken up by Peter at Pentecost (2:21) and by Paul (Romans 10:13). Readers weigh the parts differently. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran readers take the washing as what God does in baptism; Churches of Christ, who do not use the word "sacrament," also teach that sins are forgiven at baptism. Reformed readers see baptism as the sign and seal of a washing done by Christ's blood and received by faith. Baptists and many evangelicals put the weight on "calling on his name," the faith that baptism expresses, and note that Paul had already met the risen Jesus three days before. See the Where Christians differ card. Paul uses the same verb in 1 Corinthians 6:11, reminding the Corinthians that they were washed.
orig: βάπτισαι καὶ ἀπόλουσαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου (baptisai kai apolousai tas hamartias sou)

a: As I prayed in the temple, a trance came over me
p: Only this speech tells of a vision in the temple. Chapter 9 gives a different reason for Paul's leaving Jerusalem.
b: In 9:26–30 Paul leaves Jerusalem because Greek-speaking Jews try to kill him and the believers send him to Tarsus. Here he leaves because the Lord told him to in a vision. The two fit easily: a threat and a vision can come together, and Paul's letters speak of visions and revelations from the Lord (2 Corinthians 12:1–4) and of a short first visit to Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18). The setting matters for this crowd. Paul received his mission to the Gentiles while praying in their own temple, like Isaiah, who saw the Lord there and was sent (Isaiah 6:1–9). He is saying he did not turn from the temple; it was there that God sent him out.

a: Stephen, your witness
p: The Greek martys means "witness." Here it begins to carry the sense "martyr," one whose witness costs his life.
b: Martys in Greek is a witness, someone who tells what he has seen; Paul has just been called a witness (22:15). By the second century it had come to mean one who bears witness by dying, a martyr. Many think this verse, with Revelation 2:13 and 17:6, shows the shift beginning, since Stephen's witness and his blood are named together. Paul's confession matches 8:1, which uses the same verb, syneudokeō, "agree, approve," to say that Saul approved of Stephen's killing. He tells this crowd plainly that he was once on their side.
orig: Στεφάνου τοῦ μάρτυρός σου (Stephanou tou martyros sou)

a: I am going to send you out to the Gentiles, far away
t: The word that ended the speech
p: The crowd listened until Paul said God sent him to the Gentiles. Why was that the breaking point?
b: Jews of the time made converts and welcomed God-fearing Gentiles, so the mere idea of teaching Gentiles was not outrageous. What made the crowd explode was the setting and the charge. They had just been told Paul brought a Gentile into the inner courts (21:28). Now he claimed that in this very temple God had sent him away from Jerusalem to the nations, as if God had turned from them. To many, it sounded like the charge proved. Paul himself saw his Gentile mission as for Israel's sake, not against it (Romans 11:13–14). "Far away" may echo Isaiah's promise: "Peace, peace, to the one who is far and the one who is near" (Isaiah 57:19), taken up at 2:39 and in Ephesians 2:17.

a: It was never right for him to live
t: "He should never have been allowed to live"
p: The verb is in the past tense: he ought to have been killed long ago.
b: The Greek ou gar kathēken auton zēn uses an imperfect tense, "it was not fitting for him to live." Many take it to mean "he should have died long ago," or "it was a mistake to let him live," perhaps glancing at the commander who had rescued him. The Textus Receptus has kathēkon, "it is fitting," a present form, which the KJV follows: "it is not fit that he should live." The meaning is close either way, but the past tense is harsher.
orig: οὐ γὰρ καθῆκεν αὐτὸν ζῆν (ou gar kathēken auton zēn)

a: throwing their cloaks off, and they tossed dust up into the air
p: Gestures of outrage. The cloaks recall Stephen's death, the dust Shimei's curse on David.
b: The verb rhiptō means "throw," so the cloaks may be thrown off or tossed about. Readers have explained the gestures several ways: getting ready to stone Paul (Stephen's killers laid down their cloaks, 7:58), shaking out garments in horror at blasphemy (compare 18:6 and the tearing of clothes in Matthew 26:65), or simply wild protest. Throwing dust was a sign of cursing and of grief: Shimei threw dirt at David as he cursed him (2 Samuel 16:13), and mourners put dust on their heads (Joshua 7:6). Whatever its precise sense, the commander saw a mob about to kill.

a: to get the truth out of him under the whip
p: Romans often questioned slaves and non-citizens under torture. The whip was a brutal weapon.
b: The verb anetazō means to examine, and "with whips" (mastixin) names the method. Roman officials regularly used torture to get information from slaves and people of low status, and the commander still did not know who Paul was or what he had done. The Roman scourge (flagellum) was a whip of leather thongs, sometimes weighted with bone or metal; it was the punishment Jesus suffered before the cross (Matthew 27:26; John 19:1). Men could die from it. This was not the beating with rods that Paul had received at Philippi (16:22–23).

a: tied him with the straps
t: Tied with straps, or stretched out for the lash?
p: The Greek can mean they tied him with leather thongs, or stretched him out "for the whips."
b: Proeteinan auton tois himasin could mean "they stretched him forward with the thongs," that is, tied him in place, or "they stretched him out for the thongs," meaning the lashes of the whip, which were also himantes. Both senses describe the moment just before the flogging began, and either way the prisoner was helpless when he spoke. This translation takes the straps as the cords that held him, since the next verses speak of Paul having been tied up (22:29).
orig: προέτειναν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἱμᾶσιν (proeteinan auton tois himasin)

a: Does the law let you whip a Roman
p: Roman law forbade flogging a citizen without trial. To claim citizenship falsely was a capital crime.
b: Old Roman laws (the Porcian laws, and later the Julian law on public violence) protected citizens from being beaten or tortured without trial and gave them the right of appeal. The most famous example in ancient literature is Cicero's speech against Verres, a governor who had a Roman citizen flogged in the marketplace at Messina while the man cried out, "I am a Roman citizen" (Against Verres 2.5.161–162). Paul had used the same right at Philippi, after the beating (16:37). How did anyone prove it? Citizens could carry a small folding tablet recording their registration, though we do not know whether Paul did. A false claim was punishable by death, which is why the claim alone stopped the soldiers.

a: It cost me a great deal of money to acquire this citizenship
p: Under Claudius, Roman citizenship could be bought through bribes. The commander's name, Claudius, fits.
b: The historian Cassius Dio says that under the emperor Claudius (41–54) people bought citizenship from the emperor's wife Messalina and his freedmen, so that it was first sold for large sums and later became so cheap that people joked it could be had for broken glass (Roman History 60.17.5–6). The commander's name, Claudius Lysias (23:26), suggests a Greek who took the emperor's family name when he became a citizen, as new citizens did. Paul's answer, "I was born to it," quietly outranks him. How Paul's family got citizenship is unknown. Jerome reports a tradition that his parents came from Gischala in Galilee and were taken as prisoners to Tarsus (Lives of Illustrious Men 5); if they were later freed by a Roman citizen, they would have gained citizenship that way.

a: ordered the chief priests and all the Sanhedrin to come together
t: Could a Roman officer summon the Sanhedrin?
p: Some historians doubt that a tribune could order the high council to meet. Others think the scene is plausible.
b: The Sanhedrin was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem, led by the high priest, with priests, elders and scribes, both Sadducees and Pharisees (23:6). Ernst Haenchen thought a Roman tribune could not command it to convene. A. N. Sherwin-White, a historian of Roman law, judged the scene believable: the commander did not hold a trial but called an informal hearing to learn what the charge was, as Roman officials often consulted local leaders, and the governor stood behind him. Luke calls the meeting synedrion, which can mean the formal council or simply a gathering for consultation. Note that the commander "brought Paul down," from the Antonia to the council's meeting place.

a: I have lived as a citizen before God
p: The verb politeuomai means to live as a citizen. Paul speaks of his life as public loyalty to God.
b: Pepoliteumai, from polis "city," means "I have lived as a citizen, carried out my duties as a member of the community." Paul uses the same verb in Philippians 1:27, urging believers to live as citizens in a way worthy of the good news, and speaks of their citizenship in heaven (Philippians 3:20). Before the council of his people, he claims he has always been a loyal member of God's people. His "good conscience" (repeated in 24:16) may surprise readers who remember his persecuting days. Krister Stendahl argued that Paul, unlike later Western Christians, did not suffer from a tortured conscience: he saw his past as an error of zeal, not a burden of guilt.

a: The high priest Ananias
p: High priest about AD 47 to 59, known for greed and violence, murdered by rebels in 66.
b: This Ananias is not the Ananias of 22:12 or of 5:1. Herod of Chalcis appointed him about AD 47. Josephus says he was sent to Rome in chains in 52 over violence between Jews and Samaritans and came back cleared (Jewish War 2.243; Antiquities 20.131). He describes him as rich, and says his servants seized the tithes owed to ordinary priests by force, so that some priests starved (Antiquities 20.205–207, 213). He kept great influence after leaving office. When the revolt broke out in 66, rebels burned his house and killed him (Jewish War 2.426, 441–442). Paul's angry words in 23:3 were later read as a prophecy of this end.

a: you wall painted with whitewash
p: A crumbling wall with a fresh coat of white. Ezekiel used the image for false prophets; Jesus used a similar one.
b: Ezekiel said the false prophets cried "Peace" when there was no peace, like men smearing whitewash on a flimsy wall that God's storm would knock down (Ezekiel 13:10–16). Jesus told the scribes and Pharisees, "You resemble tombs painted with whitewash" (Matthew 23:27): clean outside, rotten inside. Paul's insult means: you look like a judge, but you are a sham, and you will fall. Hearers who knew Ananias's later murder (see 23:2) took "God will be the one to strike you" as a prophecy fulfilled.

a: you break the law and give orders for me to be struck
p: Jesus answered calmly when struck before the high priest. Paul flares up. Readers have long compared the two.
b: The law required fair judgment (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 25:1–2), and striking an accused man before a verdict broke it, as Paul says. When Jesus was slapped at his hearing he replied, "If I spoke badly, give evidence about what was bad. But if I spoke well, why are you beating me?" (John 18:23). Readers differ on Paul. Augustine, discussing the command to turn the other cheek, argued that Paul's words were a prophecy, not a curse spoken in anger (The Lord's Sermon on the Mount 1.19.58). Others see a flash of human temper, which Paul at once corrects (23:5). Jesus' own saying about turning the other cheek (Matthew 5:39) is sometimes set against Paul here; others note that Jesus, too, protested an unjust blow. Luke reports it without judging.

a: I had no idea he was the high priest
p: The high priest was presiding. Readers have offered at least four explanations.
b:
• Poor eyesight. Some connect Paul's eye trouble (Galatians 4:15; 6:11) with his failure to recognize Ananias.
  • An informal meeting. If the commander called the session (22:30), the high priest may not have been in his robes or in the presiding seat, and Paul, long away from Jerusalem, did not know his face.
  • Irony. Many readers hear sarcasm: "I did not think a man who acts like that could be the high priest."
  • A real apology. Paul admits his mistake and corrects himself from the law, showing that he does respect it, the very thing he has been accused of breaking.
The last fits the way Paul quotes Scripture against himself, and fits Luke's picture of a law-keeping Paul.

a: You will not say bad things about a ruler of your people
p: Paul quotes the law in its Greek form. The site's Plain of Exodus reads "do not curse a leader of your people."
b: The quotation follows the Septuagint of Exodus 22:28 (22:27 in Hebrew), "you will not speak evil of a ruler of your people." The Hebrew says, "Do not treat God with contempt, and do not curse a leader of your people" (Exodus 22:28). The Hebrew nasi' means a tribal leader or chief, which the Greek renders archōn, "ruler." Jewish interpreters applied the verse to judges and leaders generally. Paul applies it to the high priest, the ruler of the council, even an unworthy one.

a: I am a Pharisee
p: Paul splits the council by naming the resurrection. Some call it a clever ploy; others say he named the real issue.
b: Paul calls himself a Pharisee in his letters too (Philippians 3:5). Readers have judged his move here in different ways. Some, from the early church on, admired it as wise: Jesus told his followers to be "shrewd as snakes" (Matthew 10:16). Others think it less than honest, since Paul's case was about Jesus, not the resurrection in general. A third view, now common, says the point is not a trick at all: for Paul the resurrection of Jesus was the first sign of the general resurrection Israel hoped for, so the hope of Israel and the gospel are one claim. He returns to it in every defense (24:15, 21; 26:6–8; 28:20). Luke notes elsewhere that some Pharisees had become believers (15:5).

a: because of hope and the resurrection of the dead
p: Two nouns joined by "and" probably name one thing: the hope that the dead will rise.
b: Peri elpidos kai anastaseōs nekrōn, "about hope and resurrection of the dead," is most likely a hendiadys, one idea expressed with two words joined by "and": "the hope of the resurrection." Paul ties his trial to Israel's hope again before Felix (24:15), before Agrippa (26:6–7) and in Rome, where he says he wears his chain for the hope of Israel (28:20). The translation keeps both words so readers can follow the theme.
orig: περὶ ἐλπίδος καὶ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν (peri elpidos kai anastaseōs nekrōn)

a: no resurrection, no angel, and no spirit
p: The Sadducees accepted the books of Moses, which mention angels. So what does "no angel, no spirit" mean?
b:
The Sadducees denied the resurrection (Matthew 22:23; Josephus, Antiquities 18.16; Jewish War 2.165). Nothing outside this verse says they denied angels, and since they accepted the five books of Moses, where angels appear (Genesis 19:1; 28:12), the claim is puzzling. Views:
  • Taken as it stands. They rejected the developed belief in angels and spirits of their day, or explained the Torah's angels away.
  • No life after death in angelic or spirit form. David Daube argued that "angel" and "spirit" here are forms in which the dead were thought to exist before the resurrection (compare 12:15, "It is his angel"). The Sadducees denied resurrection in any form.
  • Luke's simplification for Gentile readers, or a reflection of Pharisee polemic.

a: Pharisees affirm both
p: Luke lists three things and says the Pharisees affirm "both." The Greek word can mean "all" loosely.
b: Ta amphotera normally means "both of two." Luke has named three: resurrection, angel, spirit. Either "both" is used loosely for "all of them," as it sometimes is in Greek papyri and in 19:16, or Luke thinks of two subjects: the resurrection, and angel-or-spirit as one. The second fits Daube's reading in the note just before. This translation keeps "both" so readers can see the puzzle.

a: We find nothing bad about this man
p: Paul's trials, like Jesus', bring one verdict of innocence after another.
b: Pilate found Jesus not guilty three times (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). Paul's hearings echo this: the Pharisee scribes here, Claudius Lysias (23:29), Festus (25:25) and Agrippa (26:31–32) all say he has done nothing deserving death. Luke was writing for readers who needed to know that the Christian leader in Roman chains was not a criminal. The scribes' unfinished sentence ("if a spirit spoke to him, or an angel...") is on the variants list; the Byzantine text finishes it with Gamaliel's warning against "fighting against God" (5:39).

a: the commander feared they would pull Paul apart
p: Once again Roman soldiers save Paul from his own people. Luke tells this pattern often.
b: The commander rescues Paul three times in three chapters: from the mob (21:32), from the scourge after he learns Paul is a citizen (22:29), and from the council (23:10); then from the plot (23:23). In Acts the Roman authorities are often fair, if self-interested (18:14–16; 19:35–41). Some scholars see apologetic purpose: Luke shows Roman readers that the empire had no quarrel with Christianity. Others warn against overreading. Luke also shows Felix taking bribes (24:26) and Festus playing politics (25:9), and his heroes still end up in chains.

a: you must bear witness in Rome too
p: The Greek dei, "it is necessary," is Luke's word for God's plan. Rome is now sure.
b: Luke uses dei, "it must," for things required by God's purpose: the Messiah must suffer (Luke 24:26), Scripture must be fulfilled (Luke 22:37), and Paul must see Rome (19:21; 27:24). The Lord's words here answer Paul's own plan in 19:21 and carry the story to its last scene, Paul preaching in Rome openly and unhindered (28:31). They also complete the outline of 1:8: witnesses "to the ends of the earth." The Lord standing beside Paul at night recalls the night vision at Corinth (18:9–10) and the angel in the storm (27:23–24), and Paul's own memory of the Lord standing by him (2 Timothy 4:17).

a: They put themselves under a curse
p: The verb is anathematizō: they called down a curse on themselves if they ate before Paul was dead.
b: Anethematisan heautous, "they put themselves under an anathema," means they swore an oath that invoked God's curse on themselves if they failed (compare Saul's oath, "God do so, and more besides!" (1 Samuel 14:44)). Did they starve when the plot failed? Probably not. The Mishnah lists vows that the sages could release, including vows broken because of circumstances beyond one's control (Mishnah Nedarim 3:1, 3), and a plot foiled by a Roman escort would count. The tone of the plot fits the Sicarii of these years (21:38), who killed opponents in crowds.

a: the Jews
p: Luke means a group of more than forty plotters, not the Jewish people. The Byzantine text says "some of the Jews."
b: As in John, "the Jews" in these chapters often means a particular group in a particular place: here the forty conspirators (23:13), elsewhere the accusers from Asia (21:27) or the leaders who brought charges (22:30). Luke's same story shows other Jews on Paul's side: the tens of thousands of believing Jews (21:20), the Pharisee scribes who defend him (23:9), his own nephew (23:16). Later Christian use of such verses against the Jewish people as a whole misreads them. Copyists may already have felt the problem: the Byzantine text and the KJV read "certain of the Jews," which looks like a correction (see the variants).

a: They came to the chief priests and the elders
p: The plotters went to the chief priests and elders, not to the Pharisee scribes who had just defended Paul.
b: The plotters approach the priestly leaders and the lay aristocracy, the groups Luke links with the Sadducees (4:1; 5:17). The scribes of the Pharisees, who had just said they found nothing wrong in Paul (23:9), are not mentioned. Josephus shows high priests of these years hiring armed men and using violence against rivals (Antiquities 20.181, 206–207), so Luke's picture of a high-priestly circle open to such a plan is not far-fetched. The plan's cover story was a further hearing "to look into his case more closely" (23:15), which used the commander's own wish to know the facts (22:30).

a: Paul's nephew, his sister's son
p: The only mention of Paul's relatives in the New Testament, apart from the kinsmen greeted in Romans 16.
b: We know almost nothing of Paul's family. This verse shows that he had a married sister whose son lived in Jerusalem, which fits Paul's own upbringing there (22:3). How the young man heard of the plot is not said; perhaps through family links to priestly or Pharisee circles. That he could walk into the barracks and see Paul fits Roman military custody, in which friends and relatives were often allowed to visit and bring food (compare 24:23; 27:3). Romans 16:7, 11, 21 greet some of Paul's kinsmen (syngeneis), which may mean relatives or simply fellow Jews.

a: two hundred spearmen
p: No one is sure what dexiolaboi were. The word is not found in any Greek text older than Acts.
b: Dexiolabous means something like "right-hand takers." It does not appear in any earlier Greek writing, and later examples are few. Guesses include spearmen or javelin men (holding the weapon in the right hand), light-armed troops, or men who led spare horses (taking them by the right hand). Copyists were puzzled too: Codex Alexandrinus (02) has a different word, dexiobolous, "right-hand throwers," as reported in the NA28 apparatus (with minuscule 33). The total escort, 470 men, was large for one prisoner, perhaps half of the garrison. Some think Luke exaggerates; others note the danger of a night road with forty sworn assassins, and the commander's fear of blame (see the variant on 23:24).

a: Felix, the governor
p: A former slave who rose to govern Judea about AD 52–59. Tacitus despised him.
b: Felix was a freedman of the emperor's family and the brother of Pallas, Claudius' powerful treasury secretary. He governed Judea from about 52 until about 59 or 60. Tacitus wrote that he "exercised the power of a king with the mind of a slave" (Histories 5.9) and that he thought he could do any wrong and get away with it (Annals 12.54). Josephus tells of his harsh rule, his campaigns against bandits and the Egyptian prophet (21:38), and his marriage to Drusilla, daughter of Agrippa I, whom he took from her husband (Antiquities 20.141–144). On Felix and Paul, see chapter 24.

a: along these lines
t: How did Luke know what the letter said?
p: Luke introduces the letter with "having this form" or "to this effect." Did he have a copy?
b: The Greek echousan ton typon touton can mean "having this content" or "in this form." The letter would have been read when Paul's case was heard by Felix, and Paul or his friends may have learned its contents then (24:22). Ancient historians, however, freely composed letters and speeches that fit the occasion, and Luke's phrase may admit as much. The letter's careful tilt in its writer's favor (see 23:27) has persuaded many that it reflects a real document, or at least a sharp sense of how such men wrote. It is one of two letters quoted in full in Acts; the other is the Jerusalem decree (15:23–29).

a: most excellent
p: The title kratistos was used for men of high rank. Luke used it for Theophilus.
b: Kratistos, Latin egregius, was a courtesy title for high officials, especially of the equestrian order, the second rank of Roman society. Paul uses it for Festus (26:25), and Tertullus for Felix (24:3). Luke gave Theophilus the same title when he addressed his Gospel to him (Luke 1:3), which suggests Theophilus was a man of standing, perhaps an official. The letter's opening, "to... greetings" (chairein), is the normal form of a Greek letter, as in 15:23 and James 1:1.

a: since I had found out that he is a Roman
p: The commander learned Paul was a Roman only after nearly flogging him. His letter reverses the order.
b: In the letter, Lysias rescues Paul because he is a Roman. In the story, he arrested him, chained him and ordered him flogged, and found out only later (22:25–29). He also leaves out the flogging order. Commentators enjoy the touch: a junior officer writing to his superior puts himself in the best light. It also shows Luke's art: a reader who knows the story sees the spin.

a: disputes about their law
p: To a Roman officer, the case was an internal Jewish argument, not a crime.
b: Lysias says the charges concern "disputes about their law" and nothing deserving death or chains. Gallio said the same at Corinth (18:14–15), and Festus will say it to Agrippa (25:18–20, 25). Many scholars see here one of Luke's aims: to show Roman readers that Christianity was not a threat to public order, but a dispute within Judaism, then a legal religion. Others read the stress on Paul's innocence as aimed at Christian readers troubled that their great apostle died a Roman prisoner. The two aims can go together.

a: as far as Antipatris
p: Antipatris lay about 35 to 40 miles from Jerusalem. The infantry turned back there; the cavalry went on to Caesarea.
b: Herod the Great rebuilt the town and named it for his father, Antipater (Josephus, Antiquities 16.143). It stood where the hill country meets the coastal plain, on the road to Caesarea, which lay about 25 miles further. Once past the hills, the danger of ambush was over, so the foot soldiers could return. Covering 35 to 40 miles in one night is a very hard march, and some think Luke has compressed the timing; others note that the soldiers were moving fast for a reason.

a: asked which province Paul came from
p: Roman law let a governor send a case to the prisoner's home province. Felix chose to keep it.
b: A governor could try a case where the offense took place, or send the accused to the governor of his home province. Cilicia at this time was attached to the large province of Syria, whose legate was Felix's superior. Sherwin-White suggests Felix asked so he could decide whether to pass the case on, and kept it because sending a minor case to the legate of Syria would be a nuisance. Jesus was sent from Pilate to Herod because he was a Galilean (Luke 23:6–7), a similar move.

a: Herod's Praetorium
p: The governor's headquarters at Caesarea was the palace Herod the Great built on a point of land by the sea.
b: Praetorium was the Latin word for a commander's headquarters, used for the governor's residence. At Caesarea it was the palace Herod the Great built on a rocky point jutting into the sea, south of the harbor. Archaeologists have excavated it, with a pool in its lower terrace. Paul was held there, not in a dungeon, which fits the light custody of 24:23. He would stay for two years (24:27).
